newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel says part of tax reform could come in 1998.
newsitem.headline: Waigel says part of tax reform could come in 1998.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Sunday part of the coalition's comprehensive tax reform could be implemented in 1998, one year earlier than originally planned.

But the bulk of the reforms will have to wait until 1999 for administrative reasons, Waigel said after a closed meeting of a commission set up by the coalition parties to draft proposals for a radical simplification of Germany's tax system.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition partners, the Free Democrats (FDP), and opposition Social Democrats have been urging an early realisation of the plans.
The aim is to lower income tax rates and broaden the tax base by eliminating many tax breaks, to cut the burden on taxpayers by a net 30 billion marks.
The commission is due to make its final proposals to the cabinet on December 11.
Waigel said the commission's work was about three-quarters complete. It made great progress in the session, and would meet again on Tuesday, he said.
It did not discuss the timetable, but rather the question of what tax write-offs could be eliminated and how much that would bring state coffers, he said.

FDP parliamentary faction leader Hermann Otto Solms said in a radio interview he hoped the coalition would begin the tax reform in 1998 alongside a planned cut in the unpopular solidarity surcharge, which is intended to finance east German reconstruction.
The highest income tax rate is expected to be cut to about 35 percent from the current 53 percent, and the lowest rate to about 20 percent.
